MEAGHER_LHI_BRYOPHYTES  (1) 
Asterella drummondii (Taylor) R.M.Schust. ex D.G.Long
Fimbriaria drummondii Hook.f. & Taylor, London J. Bot. 3: 574 (1844), nom. nud.; Fimbriaria
drummondii Hook.f & Taylor in Gottsche, Lindenb. & Nees, Syn. Hep. 566, 791 (1846) nom. nud.;
Fimbriaria drummondii Taylor, London J. Bot. 5: 412 (1846); Asterella drummondii (Hook.f. & Taylor)
R.M.Schust., J. Hattori Bot. Lab. 26: 298 (1963), nom. inval.; Asterella drummondii (Taylor) R.M.Schust.
ex D.G.Long, J. Bryol. 21: 76 (1999)
Type: Swan River Colony, without specific locality, Drummond s.n., date unknown (before
1846); Gunn s.n., Tasmania without specific locaility, date unknown (before 1846); herbarium
location unknown.
Description: This species was described comprehensively by Scott (1985).
Illustrations: Scott (1985, Figures 25, 26).
Habitat: Soil in dry situations.
Distribution on LHI: Known recently only from the western face of Mt Gower; an earlier
record is without a specific locality.
Total distribution: Australia, ?New Zealand.
Discussion: Asterella drummondii was first reported from Lord Howe Island by Stephani and
Watts (1914) as A. subplana (see discussion below).
The original description (as Fimbriaria drummondii) by Thomas Taylor was based on two very
disjunct collections, one by James Drummond from Swan River Colony (Perth) and one by
Thomas Gunn from Tasmania. Schuster (1963) made an invalid combination in transferring it to
Asterella. Long (1999) subsequently validated the name Asterella drummondii, although citing
the authorship for the nomen nudum incorrectly (this does not affect the validity of his new
combination).

                                                                                176
Asterella subplana (Steph.) R.M.Schust. was reported from Lord Howe Island by Stephani and
Watts (1914), as Fimbriaria subplana Steph. I have little doubt that A. subplana is identical to
A. drummondii and here treat it as such, but without formalisng the synonymy. I also suspect
that Asterella australis, currently considered to be endemic to New Zealand, is identical to
A. drummondii. If this is the case then the name Asterella australis would have priority.
The only species known from New Caledonia is Asterella vulcanica (Schiffn.) Pandé,
K.P.Srivast. and Sultan Khan ex Kachroo and Bapna (Thouvenot et al. 2011).

Plagiochasma Lehm. & Lindenb.
Bischler (1979) revised Plagiochasma for Asia an Oceania and recognised only Plagiochasma
rupestre var. rupestre from Australia. Plagiochasma differs from Asterella most obviously in
having the sex organs in two or more receptacles situated along the dorsal midline of the thallus.

Plagiochasma rupestre (J.R.Forst. & G. Forst.) Steph. var. rupestre
Aytonia rupestris J.R.Forst. & G.Forst., Char. Gen. Pl. 148 (1775), Plagiochasma rupestre (J.R.Forst. &
G. Forst.) Steph., Bull. Herb. Boissier 6(10): 783 (1898)
Type: Madeira, Funchal, Quinta do Bo Sucesso, Sérgio & Nóbrega 3873, neotype LISU fide
Bischler and Sérgio (1984 (not seen), isotype PC, BM, G, MADJ (not seen).
Plagiochasma rupestre var. rupestre is usually easily recognisable because sex organs are
almost always present. Sterile specimens can be distinguished from Asterella by having some
ventral scales distinctly bilobed.
Description: This species was described comprehensively by Bischler (1979) and Perold
(1995).
Illustration: Perold (1995, Figure 1A–N).
Habitat: Soil in dry situations.
Distribution on LHI: Known only from a cave on the western face of Mt Gower.
Total distribution: Circumglobal.
Discussion: Plagiochasma rupestre var. rupestre and Asterella drummondii are sympatric on
Lord Howe Island, perhaps reflecting the limited suitable habitat there. Plagiochasma rupestre
var. volkii Bischl. is known only from southern Africa, Peru and Argentina (Perold 1995). It has
long-acuminate, colourless appendages on the ventral scales, and slightly larger spores.
